boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Second-order construct combining 4 dimensions (Information exchange, Relational activities, Coordination/negotiation, Mediation/facilitation; Table 2 pp. 414-415: alpha = 0.968, CR = 0.968).
boundary_spanning_measures.specific_measure_used: Yan et al. (2020), Ancona and Caldwell (1992), Henttonen et al. (2016), and Van Meerkerk and Edelenbos (2014)
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: All the items for this study, presented in Table 2, were measured using a 7-point Likert scale. The choices for the boundary spanning measurement scale ranged from 1 (“very little involvement”) to 7 (“involvement to a great extent”). Boundary Spanning Activity (Cronbach's alpha (α) = 0.968; Composite reliability (CR) = 0.968; Average variance extracted (AVE) = 0.684) Information collection and knowledge (IK) exchange activities: Partly adapted from Yan et al. (2020), Ancona and Caldwell (1992), Henttonen et al. (2016), and Van Meerkerk and Edelenbos (2014). Relational activities (RA): Partly based on Walter et al. (2006) and Van Meerkerk and Edelenbos (2014). Coordination and negotiation (CN) activities: Partly based on Walter et al. (2006), Ancona and Caldwell (1992), and Van Meerkerk and Edelenbos (2018b). Mediation and facilitation (MF) of collaboration: Partly adapted from Ancona and Caldwell (1992) and Jehn and Mannix (2001).

non_bs_measures.source_quote: Role conflict and role ambiguity were also measured with 1 indicating “strongly disagree” to 7 indicating “strongly agree.” Role conflict (RCON) (α = 0.742; CR = 0.749; AVE = 0.504) Adapted from Babin and Boles (1996).

Role conflict and role ambiguity were also measured with 1 indicating “strongly disagree” to 7 indicating “strongly agree.” Role ambiguity (RAMB) (α = 0.816; CR = 0.826; AVE = 0.557) Adapted from Babin and Boles (1996).

non_bs_measures.specific_measure_used: Adapted from Van Meerkerk and Edelenbos (2018b)
non_bs_measures.source_quote: The items for the organizational conditions investigated how they experienced their role within the collaboration of the specified project and it was measured by checking the extent to which the respondent was in agreement with the item scaling from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”). Top-management support (TMP) (α = 0.854; Composite reliability (CR) = 0.857; AVE = 0.667) Adapted from Van Meerkerk and Edelenbos (2018b).

The items for the organizational conditions investigated how they experienced their role within the collaboration of the specified project and it was measured by checking the extent to which the respondent was in agreement with the item scaling from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”). Co-worker support (CWS) (α = 0.933; CR = 0.935; AVE = 0.783) Adapted from Hammer et al. (2004).

The items for the organizational conditions investigated how they experienced their role within the collaboration of the specified project and it was measured by checking the extent to which the respondent was in agreement with the item scaling from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”). Role autonomy (RAUTO) (α = 0.876; CR = 0.875; AVE = 0.701) Adapted from Tummers and Bekkers (2014).

non_bs_measures.report_type_note: 5-category ordinal scale in Table 1 (1 = 1-5 yrs to 5 = >30 yrs).
non_bs_measures.source_quote: To determine the project and respondent characteristics, respondents were asked to fill in personal demographics, their role in the project team, the contract type, to list the amount of stakeholders involved (i.e., stakeholder complexity), and to list the related spatial developments—road construction, improving waterway network, ensuring water quality and safety, housing, development of industrial, commercial or recreational area, and landscaping—that were part of the project (i.e., spatial complexity) (cf. Verweij et al., 2013). The demographic characteristics (age, years of experience, and gender) and project characteristics (contract type, infrastructure system, stakeholder complexity, and spatial complexity) from Table 1 were tested as control variables in the model to see whether there is a significant impact of these variables on the structural model (see Figure 2).
